headline: Strait of Hormuz Reopens as Oil Collapses 34% from Peak; Canada Adds 14,000 Jobs, Unemployment Holds 6.7%
executive_summary:
The Strait of Hormuz reopened on April 17 following a temporary ceasefire agreed April 8, ending what the International Energy Agency characterized as the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, affecting 20% of global supplies.14 WTI crude collapsed from a peak near US$128/bbl on April 2 to US$83.85/bbl on April 17, a decline of approximately 34% in 15 trading days.97 Brent crude settled at US$90.38/bbl, down 9.0% in the April 17 session alone.47 The project database tracks 63 oil and gas projects ($100.2B) and 367 mining projects ($159.5B) with direct commodity price exposure.50

Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey recorded +14,000 jobs in March, a partial recovery after February's 84,000-job loss.148 National unemployment held at 6.7%, with the participation rate unchanged at 64.9% and the employment rate at 60.6%.148 Average hourly wages accelerated to +4.7% year-over-year ($37.73/hr), the fastest pace since October 2024, with workers aged 55 and older recording +5.2% and those aged 15-24 at +1.8%.148 Health care posted the largest year-over-year gain at +94,000 (+3.3%), while natural resources added 10,000 (+3.0%) in the month.148 The pipeline tracks 259 healthcare projects and 427 combined mining and oil and gas projects ($259.7B) in the affected sectors.

Canada's merchandise trade deficit widened to $5.7B in February from a revised $4.2B in January, the largest since August 2025.147 Exports rose 6.4% to $66.3B — the highest since March 2025 — while imports surged 8.4% to a record $72.1B.147 Manufacturing sales rebounded 3.6% to $71.2B in February, led by transportation equipment (+18.8%) and primary metals (+4.9% to a record $6.5B), with unfilled manufacturing orders reaching a record $117.6B.150 Housing starts fell 6.0% month-over-month to 235,852 SAAR in March, below the 255,000 consensus, while the MLS Home Price Index declined for a 16th consecutive month (-0.4% month-over-month).88

The Bloomberg-Nanos Consumer Confidence Index fell to 46.93, an 11-month low, with the expectations sub-index losing nearly 10 points over four weeks.43 The Bank of Canada rate decision on April 29 — accompanied by the Monetary Policy Report — and the federal Spring Economic Update on April 28 are the principal scheduled events in the coming week, with the March CPI release on April 20 expected to capture initial effects of the oil price surge.6270

national.analysis:
Real GDP contracted 0.2% quarter-over-quarter (-0.6% annualized) in Q4 2025, down from +0.6% in Q3, according to Statistics Canada.144 The monthly GDP print recorded a -0.6% month-over-month contraction in the latest release.157 Manufacturing GDP (NAICS 31-33) fell 1.4% month-over-month and 4.6% year-over-year, while management of companies and enterprises (NAICS 55) recorded the deepest annual contraction among 20 industries at -21.9% year-over-year.157 Construction GDP (NAICS 23) rose 1.1% month-over-month and 2.8% year-over-year, while mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction (NAICS 21) gained 1.2% month-over-month against a -0.1% annual base.157 Wholesale trade (NAICS 41) declined 1.2% month-over-month and 1.7% year-over-year; transportation and warehousing (NAICS 48-49) fell 0.7% month-over-month against a +1.6% annual base.157

The Labour Force Survey recorded +14,000 jobs in March after February's -84,000 loss, leaving unemployment unchanged at 6.7%.148 The provincial range ran from Saskatchewan at 5.0% to Newfoundland and Labrador at 9.5%.148 By industry, other services added +15,000 (+1.9%), professional services +12,000, and natural resources +10,000 (+3.0%), while finance, insurance, and real estate shed 11,000 and accommodation and food services lost 10,000 (-0.9%).148 Average hourly wages rose 4.7% year-over-year to $37.73/hr; composition-adjusted wage growth ran at +3.6%.148 Construction employment stood at 1,998,800, manufacturing at 249,600, and mining and oil and gas extraction at 350,300.153

Headline CPI registered +1.8% year-over-year in February 2026, within the Bank of Canada's 1-3% target band, with provincial dispersion spanning 9.1 percentage points from PE at +7.3% to ON at -1.8%.145 Core CPI median ran at 2.3%, shelter CPI at +1.5%, food CPI at +5.3%, and energy CPI at -14.2%.154 The March CPI release, scheduled for April 20, is expected to capture initial effects of the oil price surge from the Strait of Hormuz disruption.145

Canada's merchandise trade deficit widened to $5.7B in February from a revised $4.2B in January, the largest since August 2025.147 Exports rose 6.4% to $66.3B while imports surged 8.4% to a record $72.1B.147 Manufacturing sales rebounded 3.6% to $71.2B, led by transportation equipment (+18.8%) and primary metals (+4.9% to a record $6.5B).150 Unfilled manufacturing orders reached a record $117.6B.150 Building permits dropped 8.4% to $12.1B in February, with non-residential leading the decline at -$1.3B while residential added $135.6M.149

CMHC housing starts fell 6.0% month-over-month to 235,852 SAAR in March, below the 255,000 consensus.88 The six-month trend decreased 2.9% to 248,378.88 Year-to-date actual starts ran +9% year-over-year at 49,206 units through March.88 CREA downgraded its home sales forecast citing the oil shock but maintained a +1.5% annual price gain projection to $688,955.67 The MLS HPI declined for a 16th consecutive month at -0.4% month-over-month, and the national average home price stood at $673,084 (-0.8% year-over-year).39 The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25%, the seventh consecutive hold, with the Summary of Deliberations published April 1 noting near-term growth weaker than the January projection.6163 Market pricing reflects a 96.5% probability of a hold at the April 29 decision.62

The US Federal Reserve held the federal funds target range at 3.50-3.75%103 on March 18, maintaining a 125-150 basis point gap above the Bank of Canada overnight rate of 2.25%.61 The FOMC continues to signal one rate cut in 2026 and one in 2027.103 US unemployment stood at 4.4% in the February print.103 CAD/USD strengthened to 0.7305 on April 17, up 1.5% over the two-week period, driven in part by broader US dollar depreciation as the DXY index moved toward 98.05.44

US equity benchmarks posted record closes in the second week of the coverage window. The S&P 500 reached 7,022.95 on April 13, within 2.32% of its January 27 all-time high, after recording its best week since November.9459 The S&P 500 and Nasdaq both posted fresh record closes on April 14.94 The US Supreme Court struck down several IEEPA emergency tariffs during the period, and the administration announced a temporary 10% global tariff largely exempting CUSMA-compliant goods.16 Section 232 tariffs were restructured on April 6 with a 50% rate on core metal imports including aluminum, steel, and copper — directly affecting Canadian metal exporters.16 Canada responded on April 15 with a six-month pause on tariffs for US-origin manufacturing inputs.16

China's Q1 2026 GDP grew 5.0% year-over-year, beating the 4.8% consensus and accelerating from 4.5% in Q4 2025, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.95 Industrial production rose 6.1% year-over-year, with high-tech manufacturing up 12.5% and equipment manufacturing up 8.9%.95 Exports grew 2.5% year-over-year in March (USD terms), down sharply from +21.8% in the January-February combined period, while imports surged 27.8% in March, the strongest since November 2021.93 Factory-gate prices turned positive for the first time in more than three years on soaring commodity prices.95

China's import surge supports demand for Canadian commodity exports across iron ore, copper, potash, and energy products. The pipeline tracks 367 mining projects ($159.5B) and 63 oil and gas projects ($100.2B) with exposure to Chinese commodity demand.95 USD/CNY stood at 6.8287 on April 8, down 1.0% month-over-month and 7.0% year-over-year, reflecting yuan appreciation against the US dollar.44 The factory-gate price reversal to positive territory indicates sustained commodity price support for Canadian resource exporters, at a time when WTI has retraced 34% from its April 2 peak on the Strait of Hormuz reopening.97

provinces.analysis:
Ontario's unemployment rate held at 7.6% in the March Labour Force Survey148, unchanged from February, as Q4 2025 employment gains of +58,900 (+0.7%) absorbed into a stable base after two preceding weak quarters. The Ontario Economic Accounts for Q4 2025, released April 10, recorded real household consumption up +0.6% quarter-over-quarter, government expenditure up +0.6%, and capital investment flat at 0.0%, while goods-producing GDP contracted -1.5%.159 The Financial Accountability Office estimates full-year 2025 Ontario real GDP at 1.3%, down from 1.6% in 2024.156 The employment rate held flat at 59.7% while the participation rate carried at 64.6%, 0.2 percentage points above the prior observation.148 Ontario's year-over-year CPI reading of -1.8% is the lowest provincial print in Canada and widened 0.7 percentage points below the prior reading of -1.1%, standing 3.6 percentage points below the national +1.8% figure.119

Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy tabled the Ontario Budget 2026 on March 26, raising the ten-year capital plan to $210 billion (up $9 billion from the prior framework), with $37 billion allocated for 2026-27 and approximately $64 billion over ten years for health infrastructure including roughly 50 hospital projects and 3,000 new beds.119 Infrastructure spending for 2025-28 increased $13.6 billion from the Fall Economic Statement. The budget confirmed $31 billion over ten years for highway investment, with construction underway on Highway 413 (52 km, supporting 6,000 jobs per year), the Bradford Bypass, and Highway 7 expansion between Kitchener and Guelph.74 The Ring of Fire all-season road construction is now targeted for June 2026, with roads opening November 2030 — five years ahead of the prior timeline.84

The official OEA Q4 print recorded Ontario exports at $638.7 billion (annualized, chained 2017$), up +4.3% quarter-over-quarter, while imports rose +1.2% to $610.1 billion.159 Full-year 2025 goods exports to the United States fell 4.0%, while exports to the rest of the world rose 17.0%, reflecting trade diversification as the effective tariff rate on Ontario exports exceeds 6%.156 Housing starts rose 2.3% to 67,274 units (SAAR) in March, up from 65,757 the prior month.155 Building permits stood at $2,690.8 million in the latest StatCan print.134 The project database tracks the Ontario Line ($27.4B, Under Construction), GO Expansion ($26.1B, Under Construction), the Deep Geological Repository ($26.0B, Proposed), and the Bruce Nuclear Refurbishment ($13.0B, Under Construction) as the province's largest active capital files.155

provinces.analysis:
Quebec's unemployment rate fell 0.5 percentage points to 5.4% in March148, though the decline reflects fewer active job seekers rather than net hiring — employment was little changed after a -57,000 loss in February. The participation rate edged down 0.1 percentage points to 64.4%, while the employment rate rose 0.2 percentage points to 60.9%.148 Quebec City CMA posted unemployment of 2.6%, the lowest metropolitan reading in Canada.148 The Institut de la statistique du Québec recorded Q4 2025 real GDP at -0.1% quarter-over-quarter, with the 2026 GDP forecast at 1.1%.156

The Quebec Budget 2026-2027, tabled during week one of this edition window, committed $167 billion in the ten-year Quebec Infrastructure Plan (QIP) over 2026-2036, of which 71% ($105.8 billion) is designated for asset maintenance.119 The QIP allocates $35.7 billion for roads, $24.7 billion for health, $23.5 billion for education, $12.8 billion for transit, and $8.9 billion for IT infrastructure.119 An additional $1.7 billion is earmarked for economic transformation initiatives. The province also announced an $8 billion Transport Plan for 2026-2028 covering road, maritime, rail, and airport infrastructure, with 77% directed toward asset maintenance.119

Manufacturing GDP in U.S.-trade-reliant industries contracted approximately 4% between December 2024 and November 202574, as the effective tariff rate on Quebec exports to the United States exceeds 6%. CPI ran at +0.6% year-over-year in February, down 0.1 percentage points from the prior reading.84 Housing starts rose 2.8% to 53,461 units (SAAR).155 The project database tracks the Parc éolien Chamouchouane wind farm ($9.0B, Proposed), the Montreal Metro Blue Line Extension ($4.9B, Under Construction, completion 2031), the TES Canada Hydrogen facility in Shawinigan ($4.0B, Under Review), and the Quebec City Tramway ($3.8B, Under Construction, completion 2033).134 The Timiskaming Dam-Bridge environmental assessment decision deadline was extended on March 9.155

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
Nova Scotia's unemployment rate fell 0.5 percentage points to 6.6% in March, with employment rising 3,900 (+0.7%).148 Halifax CMA unemployment stood at 6.1%, up 0.2 percentage points.148 Halifax GDP grew 2.3% in 2025, with a forecast of 1.5% for 2026.156 The participation rate carried at 61.3% and the employment rate at 57.0%.119 CPI rose 0.2 percentage points to +1.7% year-over-year in February.119

The Nova Scotia Legislature concluded its session on April 9 (week two of this edition window), passing Budget 2026-27 and the Powering the Economy Act, which establishes a regulatory framework for offshore wind, geothermal, hydrogen, and carbon storage.74 Offshore wind bid requirements include a $250,000 refundable deposit, $750,000 non-refundable fee, and $7,000 per MW per year.74 Canada and Nova Scotia signed a new assessment agreement on March 27 implementing the "one project, one review" framework.84 The province allocated $300 million for 1,430 homes including 930 units at Shannon Park, and $873.8 million for 5,700 long-term care spaces by 2032.74

Housing starts totalled 7,146 units (SAAR) in March, down 1.5% from the prior month, following a 2025 provincial record of 9,760 units.155 The province introduced a First Time Homebuyers Pilot enabling 2% down payments via provincial credit unions.74 Bear Head Energy ($8.0B, Proposed) is the province's largest energy project, while the NS Capital Plan 2026-27 ($3.5B) includes health and housing commitments. CFB Halifax Upgrade ($1.2B) and 14 Wing Greenwood Hangar ($648M) reflect federal defence investment in the province.134 Building permits stood at $242.9 million.155

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
Newfoundland and Labrador's unemployment rate rose 0.3 percentage points to 9.5% in March — the highest provincial reading in Canada — despite ongoing offshore project ramp-ups.148 The offshore petroleum sector accounts for approximately 20% of provincial GDP and 55% of exports.156 The participation rate carried at 58.1%, up 0.5 percentage points from the prior observation, and the employment rate at 52.7%, up 0.4 percentage points.119 CPI rose 0.5 percentage points to +2.3% year-over-year in February.119

The Province reached a benefits agreement with Equinor and BP on the Bay du Nord deepwater oil project during week one — the first standalone offshore development since Hebron. The agreement covers 3 million fabrication hours, 31 million person-hours over 25 years, and up to $6.4 billion in Phase 1 revenue, including royalties, local benefits, and an equity option.74 West White Rose topsides and concrete gravity structure installation and drilling are underway, extending the White Rose field's production life.84 The Point Rousse Port received an IAAC early decision on February 18 confirming no further assessment is required.155

Offshore employment totalled 20,500 jobs (8.4% of the provincial workforce) in 2024, with wages ranging from $80,000 to over $150,000.156 Housing starts edged up 2.4% to 1,223 units (SAAR) and building permits stood at $74.1 million.134155 The Grassy Point LNG facility ($10.0B, Proposed), Bay du Nord ($6.4B, Approved), and Kami mining project ($3.86B, Under Review) compose the province's deepest project pipeline, with tariff exposure below 1% given the offshore orientation of NL exports.156

provinces.analysis:
Yukon's unemployment held at 3.9% in March, unchanged from February and the lowest territorial rate.148 The 2024 annual GDP contracted 3.3%.156 CPI, housing starts, and participation rate are not published at the territorial level. Mineral spending in the territory totalled $313 million in 2025, of which $241.7 million was exploration expenditure.119

The federal and territorial governments approved the Kudz Ze Kayah copper-lead-zinc mine on April 15 (week two of this edition window), despite opposition from the Kaska Nation.119 BMC Minerals plans to mine 2 million tonnes per year over 10 years, which would make it Canada's largest zinc producer. The territory tightened mining approval timelines and launched an online bonding calculator and live project tracking system during the two-week window.74 The Yukon-BC Grid Connect is in early planning stages, with the North Canol corridor tied to both the Macmillan Pass and Mactung mineral deposits.119

The Casino Mine ($3.62B, Proposed) — a copper-gold-molybdenum project — is the territory's largest proposed mining development. provinces.analysis:
The Northwest Territories recorded the largest unemployment increase nationally in March, surging 0.8 percentage points to 6.1% from 5.3% in February.148 The spike reflects the ongoing wind-down of the territory's diamond mining sector. The Diavik diamond mine completed final production after 23 years and 150 million carats, marking the closure of one of three mines that at peak employed over 1,500 NWT residents and generated approximately 20% of territorial GDP.156

The diamond industry has channelled over $30 billion into the Canadian economy over 25 years, of which $20 billion flowed through the NWT.156 Two diamond mines remain operational: Gahcho Kue (De Beers, producing until 2031) and Ekati (projected operations to 2040).156 The Tlicho Government, Yellowknives Dene First Nation, and GNWT signed a partnership agreement to support workers and communities through the structural transition.119 Territorial leaders are pivoting to critical minerals — a strategy requiring more but smaller mines than the diamond model.156

The 2024 annual GDP contracted 1.1%.119 CPI and housing starts are not published at the territorial level. The Mackenzie Valley Highway ($2.0B, Approved) and Taltson Hydro Expansion ($2.0B, Approved) are the territory's largest approved infrastructure projects. The Pine Point lead-zinc mine ($653M, Under Review) represents the critical minerals pivot in practice. Federal Arctic Defence spending ($35.0B, Proposed) would include NWT components.74

provinces.analysis:
Nunavut's unemployment rate stands at approximately 13.8% (three-month average through January 2026) — the highest rate in Canada — reflecting structural barriers to employment in remote communities despite active mining operations.148 The March rate is not separately enumerated for Nunavut. The 2024 annual GDP grew 7.5%, the strongest rate among all provinces and territories.156 CPI and housing starts are not published at the territorial level.

The territory hosts three gold mines producing over 1.2 million ounces per year, alongside world-class iron ore deposits and a growing critical minerals pipeline.119 Baffinland concluded Inuit consultation on the Steensby Component during this edition window, with rail-and-port construction planned for 2026.119 The Baffinland Steensby Expansion ($3.0B, Approved) would create the territory's first railway. B2Gold's Goose Mine installed a CleanDesign hybrid energy system, reducing diesel consumption by approximately 4,000 litres per day.119

The Grays Bay Port and Road project proposes a 900-km road connecting the Arctic coast to southern infrastructure, part of a broader federal commitment of over $40 billion for northern infrastructure and critical minerals development.74 The 750 Homes Initiative ($480M, Under Construction) addresses acute housing need in the territory's communities. Back River Gold ($610M, Under Construction) and federal Northern Defence spending ($32.0B, Proposed) round out the project pipeline. Nunavut land-use plan negotiations continue amid increased mining interest.84

goodsIndustries.analysis:
Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting sector GDP printed -1.4% month-over-month and +5.4% year-over-year in the January 2026 StatCan GDP-by-industry release, the strongest annual reading among the 20 tracked NAICS industries.1 China imposed a 75.8% duty on Canadian canola seed during the two-week window, layering atop the 100% tariff on canola oil and meal levied in March; canola settled at CAD$711.14/tonne, down 2.07% month-over-month but up 6.40% year-over-year.2 Wheat prices stood approximately 7% above five-year lows, with TD Economics forecasting a 5% year-over-year increase for 2026, still below the 10-year average.3 The natural resources sector added 10,000 jobs in the March 2026 Labour Force Survey.4

Crop production GDP rose 8.9% year-over-year, contrasting with forestry and logging at -7.5% year-over-year; fishing, hunting and trapping gained 0.5% year-over-year.1 The federal government announced investment in low-carbon agrichemicals — a bio-electric process converting CO2 and water into formic acid and hydrogen peroxide for agricultural use — while B.C. opened a $2.5M round of its On-Farm Technology Adoption Program, which has awarded $6.4M to 134 farm projects since 2023.5,6 Offsetting these supports, the federal government closed three Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada research and development centres in Ontario, Quebec, and Alberta, plus four satellite research farms.7

Lumber prices fell to US$570/thousand board feet, near a one-month low, as U.S. single-family housing starts collapsed 14.2% and building permits declined 5.4%.8 U.S. Section 232 tariffs and higher antidumping and countervailing duty rates increase Canadian producers’ costs by an estimated 25–30%.8 The federal government committed $700M in loan guarantees and $500M for product diversification to the forest sector, alongside support for a new advanced wood manufacturing facility.9 The project database tracks 17 agriculture and forestry projects totalling $5.47B declared, of which 12 forestry projects carry $4.73B in parsed value.10 If China’s canola tariffs remain at current levels and U.S. softwood duties finalize near the preliminary 25% in August, the 17 tracked projects would carry updated market-access assumptions.

goodsIndustries.analysis:
Mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction sector GDP printed +1.2% month-over-month and -0.1% year-over-year in the January 2026 StatCan release.1 Crude oil prices fell sharply during the two-week window: Brent dropped from approximately US$107/bbl in week one to US$99.36/bbl by April 13, a 7.5% intra-period decline, while WTI plunged over 10% in a single session during week two to below US$84/bbl as ceasefire negotiations progressed.2,3 Copper recovered from below US$5.80/lb in week one to US$6.07/lb by period close, up 4.91% month-over-month and 29.97% year-over-year.4 Gold traded in the US$3,900–4,000/oz range, down approximately 7% from its $4,400 peak.5

Oil and gas extraction GDP rose 0.9% year-over-year, while mining excluding oil and gas contracted 4.4% year-over-year; support activities for mining gained 2.6% year-over-year.1 The Canada Energy Regulator issued 659 new well licences in March 2026, up 48% from 446 a year ago, with the full-year 2026 forecast at 5,709 wells (+3% year-over-year).6 U.S. restructured Section 232 tariffs took effect April 6, applying 50% duties on the full customs value of steel, aluminum, and copper articles, increasing costs for Canadian metal producers.7

The Critical Minerals Production Alliance Round 2 announced 30 new partnerships unlocking $12.1B in project capital with 12 allied partners, backed by a $2B Critical Minerals Sovereign Fund over five years and a $1.5B First and Last Mile Fund from 2026 to 2030.8 Specific projects include Frontier Lithium ($2.3M conditional), E3 Lithium Clearwater (up to $36.5M), and Cyclic Materials (up to $9.1M plus US$25M CGF equity).8 Pipeline permits for U.S.-Canada oil transportation were issued April 15, and Alberta is expected to apply for a new northwest coast oil pipeline by July 1, 2026; an Indigenous-led floating LNG terminal is nearing final investment decision.9 Mining and O&G employment stood at 350,300 in March 2026.10 The project database tracks 421 mining and oil and gas projects totalling $268.74B declared.11 If WTI stabilizes below $85/bbl and ceasefire progress continues, the 421 tracked projects would carry reduced revenue assumptions for oil sands operations, while the $12.1B Critical Minerals Alliance provides offsetting support for non-hydrocarbon mining.

Construction sector GDP printed +1.1% month-over-month and +2.8% year-over-year in the January 2026 StatCan GDP-by-industry release.1 Lumber prices fell to US$570/mbf, near a one-month low, as U.S. single-family housing starts collapsed 14.2% and building permits declined 5.4%, compressing cross-border demand and providing input cost relief for Canadian framers.2 CMHC reported March 2026 housing starts at 235,852 SAAR, down 6% from February’s 250,961; the six-month trend declined 2.9% to 248,378.3 Year-to-date actual starts were up 9% from 2025, with Montreal +26%, Vancouver +21%, and Toronto +23% year-over-year in actuals.3

Heavy and civil engineering construction GDP rose 5.8% year-over-year, the strongest goods subsector, while construction of buildings gained 1.2% and specialty trade contractors 2.8% year-over-year.1 Prime Minister Carney launched the $51B Build Communities Strong Fund on April 7, projected to boost GDP by $95B over the decade; the first project is the $64M Embleton Community Centre in Brampton, and the first tranche covers 13 projects with $300M in federal funding.4 Ontario’s 2026 budget commits more than $210B over 10 years, including $37B in 2026-27 for highways, hospitals, and transit, though capital spending is set to decline from $38.6B (2026-27) to $28.9B (2028-29).5

A CMHC study found that residential construction labour productivity declined 37.3% cumulatively between 2001 and 2023, a structural drag on housing supply capacity.6 ConstructConnect forecasts civil construction to expand by nearly 30% in 2026, while residential construction is projected to decline 5% year-over-year for the fifth straight year.7 Construction employment stood at 1,998,800 in March 2026.8 The project database tracks 2,196 construction-category projects totalling $258.36B declared.9 If the Build Communities Strong Fund flows on the announced cadence and Ontario’s $37B capital plan proceeds, the 2,196 tracked projects would carry updated funding attribution through the program window.

goodsIndustries.analysis:
Manufacturing sector GDP printed -1.4% month-over-month and -4.6% year-over-year in the January 2026 StatCan GDP-by-industry release, the steepest annual decline among goods industries.1 February 2026 manufacturing sales rose 3.6% to $71.2B, rebounding from a 3.1% decline in January; sales gained in 12 of 21 subsectors, led by transportation equipment at +18.8%.2 Capacity utilization rose from 75.4% to 77.1%, and unfilled orders reached a record $117.6B (+2.3% month-over-month), driven by aerospace products and parts at +4.2%.2

Food manufacturing GDP contracted 8.3% year-over-year, and transportation equipment manufacturing fell 10.3% year-over-year, the deepest subsector declines.1 U.S. restructured Section 232 tariffs took effect April 6, applying 50% duties on the full customs value of steel, aluminum, and copper articles; Canadian mould makers reported direct bottom-line impact from the restructuring.3,4 Canada extended relief from 25% counter-tariffs on certain U.S.-manufactured vehicles for an additional year on April 8.3

The Canadian Sovereign AI Compute Strategy launched April 15 commits up to $700M for domestic AI compute capacity and $1B for public supercomputing, generating data centre construction demand that cross-references NAICS 23 and NAICS 51.5 The data centre construction pipeline exceeds $4B: Microsoft is deploying part of a $13.72B Ontario commitment, Bell committed $1.7B in Saskatchewan, and eStruxture announced $750M in Alberta.6 Manufacturing employment stood at 249,600 in March 2026.7 The project database tracks 52 manufacturing-tagged projects totalling $67.39B declared.8 If the February manufacturing sales rebound sustains and unfilled orders continue to build, the next GDP-by-industry release may show a partial recovery, though the Section 232 restructuring introduces additional cost pressure that may offset the sales rebound.

servicesIndustries.name: Wholesale Trade
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Wholesale trade output declined 1.2% month-over-month and 1.7% year-over-year in January 2026, the steepest annual contraction in the wholesale-retail bloc.1 The GDP data lags the more current monthly wholesale trade survey, which recorded a 2.0% rebound in February to $86.8B, with five of seven subsectors posting gains.2 Motor vehicles and parts led the recovery at +6.1% to $14.4B, food, beverages, and tobacco rose 2.9% to $16.5B, and personal and household goods climbed 2.5% to a record $13.2B.2

Farm product wholesalers expanded 16.2% year-over-year, partially reflecting canola price dynamics ahead of China's 75.8% tariff on Canadian canola seed, while motor vehicle and parts wholesalers contracted 10.5% year-over-year amid cross-border trade disruptions.2,3 Saskatchewan wholesale trade rose 15.3% year-over-year in February, ranking first among provinces, while Ontario posted the largest absolute increase at 2.8% to $44.2B.3 Global Affairs Canada's Spring 2026 Quarterly Economic and Trade Report described a challenging trade environment weighing on wholesale channels, with the BoC policy rate at 2.25% defining inventory financing conditions.4

servicesIndustries.name: Retail Trade
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Retail trade output expanded 0.8% month-over-month and 2.7% year-over-year in January 2026, one of the firmer services readings.1 Statistics Canada recorded January retail sales at $70.7B, up 1.1% year-over-year, with motor vehicle dealers leading gains at +2.0% and general merchandise stores posting a fourth consecutive monthly increase.1 Moneris Q1 2026 data showed total spending declined 0.27% year-over-year while average transaction size rose 0.18%; discretionary spending excluding auto, food, and pharma rose 5.6% year-over-year.2

Consumer sentiment deteriorated across the two-week window: by mid-April, nearly half of Canadians surveyed believed the economy was faltering, only 13% expected improvement over six months, and 43% planned to reduce non-essential spending.3 Motor vehicle and parts dealers contracted 2.2% year-over-year and food and beverage stores fell 0.4%, while general merchandise stores expanded 6.4% year-over-year.1 With CPI at 1.8% year-over-year and the BoC rate at 2.25%, the pricing and borrowing environment remains relatively benign, though forward-looking sentiment indicators point to potential softening if spending reduction plans materialize.2,3

servicesIndustries.name: Transportation & Warehousing
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Transportation and warehousing output declined 0.7% month-over-month but expanded 1.6% year-over-year in January 2026.1 The federal government allocated $3.6B through the Trade Diversification Corridors Fund for infrastructure linking ports to inland markets, including the Saint John Trade Corridor upgrade covering road, rail, and logistics connections.2 Port Saint John completed its $178M modernization with DP World, increasing container capacity from 150,000 to 1,000,000 TEUs annually.3

Rail transportation contracted 2.2% year-over-year while truck transportation was near-flat at +0.1%, reflecting inland rail constraints, rising drayage costs, and enforcement-driven capacity loss reported in the cross-border freight market.3,4 Brent crude declined from approximately $107/bbl in week one to $99.36/bbl in week two, providing operating cost relief across trucking, rail, and airline subsectors where fuel is the largest variable cost.4 Transport Canada also announced a freight rate reduction initiative working with railway companies to cut rates for transporting Canadian steel and lumber interprovincially, beginning spring 2026.2 The project database tracks 601 transportation projects ($44.9B), of which 335 are in proposed status and 142 are under construction.1

servicesIndustries.name: Information & Cultural Industries
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Information and cultural industries output expanded 0.9% month-over-month and 3.2% year-over-year in January 2026, tied with finance and insurance for the strongest annual services reading.1 The federal government launched the Canadian Sovereign AI Compute Strategy on April 15, committing up to $700M for compute capacity and $1B for public supercomputing infrastructure.2 The data centre construction pipeline exceeds $4B in private investment: Bell's $1.7B Saskatchewan AI data centre, Microsoft's multi-billion-dollar Ontario deployment as part of a $13.72B commitment, and eStruxture's $750M Alberta facility.3

Publishing industries grew 6.7% year-over-year and telecommunications expanded 2.9%, as the Canadian telecom MNO market reached an estimated US$52.28B in 2026 with 5G coverage surpassing 85% of the population.4 The $3.225B Universal Broadband Fund continues subsidizing backhaul and last-mile builds targeting full rural and Indigenous coverage by 2027.4 Information, culture, and recreation employment rose 8,800 (+1%) in the March Labour Force Survey.5 The project database tracks 43 telecom and data centre projects ($3.0B), a figure that pre-dates several of the announced AI infrastructure commitments.3

servicesIndustries.name: Finance & Insurance
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Finance and insurance sector output expanded 0.5% month-over-month and 3.2% year-over-year in January 2026, tied with information and cultural industries for the strongest annual services print.1 The Bank of Canada policy rate has held at 2.25% since the March 18 decision, the seventh consecutive hold at this level, with the next decision on April 29 and no change priced at 96.5% probability.2 OSFI's 2026-27 Annual Risk Outlook identified volatile global markets, a challenging trade environment, and heightened credit risks across residential secured lending, corporate credit to non-bank financial intermediaries, and commercial real estate.3

Credit intermediation and related activities grew 2.4% year-over-year, and insurance carriers expanded 1.5%.1 Finance, insurance, real estate, and leasing posted the largest March Labour Force Survey decline at -11,000 jobs, diverging from the sector's GDP growth trajectory.5 OSFI announced a pilot program launching June 2026 to expedite bank licensing approvals for provincial institutions, fintechs, and crypto custodians, while the Consumer-Driven Banking Act advances Canada toward an open banking framework.3,4 If the BoC holds at 2.25% on April 29 as priced, credit conditions would remain stable, though OSFI's identified risks may prompt regulatory tightening in affected lending segments.2,3

servicesIndustries.name: Real Estate & Rental/Leasing
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Real estate and rental and leasing sector output declined 0.2% month-over-month but expanded 1.2% year-over-year in January 2026.1 The era of synchronized national rent inflation ended during the two-week window: Vancouver vacancy rates reached the highest levels in over 30 years, with landlords offering incentives including free rent and move-in bonuses.2 In Toronto, unsold condominium units are being converted into rental housing, increasing rental supply in the short term while reducing future ownership inventory.3 The national average home price stood at $663,828.1

Real estate services grew 1.1% year-over-year, rental and leasing services expanded 4.9%, and lessors of non-financial intangible assets contracted 3.6%.1 Edmonton's rental market continued to draw interprovincial migration from higher-cost provinces, supporting steady demand in that CMA.4 CMHC's housing market outlook indicated purpose-built rental supply is expected to rise on high numbers of units under construction, project completions, and policy incentives.5 The BoC policy rate at 2.25% defines the mortgage qualification environment; if rates hold at April 29, purchase transaction conditions would remain stable while the supply-side rental rebalancing continues.1

servicesIndustries.name: Professional, Scientific & Technical Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Professional, scientific, and technical services output was near-flat at -0.1% month-over-month and contracted 0.4% year-over-year in January 2026, though employment diverged from the GDP reading.1 The sector added 12,000 jobs in March 2026, the second-largest sectoral employment gain in the Labour Force Survey.2 Nearly 19% of the NAICS 54 workforce in western Canada and the North is over 55, and retirements are expected to increase through 2026, maintaining a tight labour market for advanced technical and engineering roles.3

Sector GDP contribution by province placed British Columbia at $26.3B, Alberta at $19.4B, Manitoba at $2.6B, Saskatchewan at $2.2B, and the territories at a combined $240M in 2024.3 Professional services demand is an intermediate input to capital project activity: the combined construction (2,196 projects, $258.4B) and utilities (824 projects, $522.9B) pipelines drive engineering, environmental consulting, and technical advisory hours.1 If the Build Communities Strong Fund ($51B), Ontario capital plan ($210B), and Sovereign AI Compute Strategy ($1.7B+) proceed on announced timelines, upstream demand for professional services would expand.2,3

servicesIndustries.name: Management of Companies & Enterprises
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Management of companies and enterprises recorded the deepest contraction among all 20 tracked industries, with output declining 4.1% month-over-month and 21.9% year-over-year in January 2026.1 This follows a 31.3% annual GDP decline in 2024, extending a multi-year contraction pattern in this subsector.1 Statistics Canada flags NAICS 55 as a small-denominator sector where single-period prints have historically fluctuated by double-digit percentages, and the current reading is classified as a statistical outlier rather than a structural trend signal.1

A DC Report analysis published April 16 noted foreign investment flows into Canada signaling renewed global confidence, though the management companies subsector has not yet reflected this in its GDP data.2 The project database carries no NAICS 55 capital tagging, as management of companies is a non-capex services sector. Given the small denominator, individual corporate events — such as headquarters relocations, holding company restructurings, or large subsidiary transactions — can move the sector GDP reading by several percentage points in either direction.1,2

servicesIndustries.name: Administrative & Waste Management Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Administrative and waste management services output declined 0.1% month-over-month and 0.2% year-over-year in January 2026, with a divergence between the contracting administrative support segment and the expanding waste management subsector.1 Administrative and support services contracted 0.8% year-over-year while waste collection grew 3.9% year-over-year, reflecting regulatory and market structure changes in the waste segment.1 Business, building, and other support services employment declined 9,500 (-1.4%) in the March Labour Force Survey.5

Ontario's Blue Box extended producer responsibility transition took full effect January 1, 2026, shifting recycling service costs from municipalities to producers and restructuring the waste management subsector's revenue model across the province.2 British Columbia's 2026 budget expanded the provincial sales tax to professional services effective 2026, affecting portions of NAICS 56 operating in B.C.3,4 The Canada waste management market was valued at US$37.02B in 2023 with a forecast to reach US$64.22B by 2030 at a 7.10% CAGR.1 The project database tracks 17 remediation and waste management projects ($1.9B).1

servicesIndustries.name: Educational Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Educational services output rose 0.5% month-over-month but contracted 1.9% year-over-year in January 2026, the largest negative annual reading in the education and health bloc.1 Approximately 16,000 sector job losses have been tracked alongside program closures and cost-cutting across Canadian institutions.2 Further reductions in international student permits are expected in 2026, with graduate-level and research-intensive institutions comparatively insulated while colleges and pathway-dependent institutions face sustained pressure on enrollment and revenue.2

Elementary and secondary schools contracted 2.2% year-over-year and universities declined 0.4%.1 Ontario's tuition freeze remains in place through the 2026-27 academic year, with a broader review of post-secondary funding underway.3 Ontario's 2026 budget committed $4.2B for education infrastructure in 2026-27, providing capital investment support that may offset enrollment-driven revenue pressures at the institutional level.4 The project database tracks 157 education projects ($14.7B), including K-12 classroom expansions, post-secondary research facilities, and workforce training centres.1 If international student permit reductions proceed as expected, enrollment declines at colleges would deepen the sector's annual GDP contraction.2

servicesIndustries.name: Health Care & Social Assistance
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Health care and social assistance sector output was flat month-over-month but expanded 2.1% year-over-year in January 2026, driven by demographic demand and sustained government capital investment in hospital infrastructure.1 Hospital construction starts are projected to reach $28.4B in 2026, with British Columbia accounting for more than $6.4B in new hospital construction starting in 2025-2026.2 Health care and social assistance employment rose 5,000 (+0.2%) in the March Labour Force Survey.5

Ambulatory health care services led subsector growth at +3.6% year-over-year, hospitals expanded 1.0%, and nursing and residential care facilities grew 0.8%.1 South Niagara Hospital — 1.3 million square feet with 469 single-patient rooms and 8 operating suites — reached structural completion in April 2026 and remains on schedule for 2028.3 The University Hospital of Northern British Columbia Phase 1 ($103M) is completing in 2026, with Phase 2 ($1.58B patient tower) construction to begin fall 2026.2 Ontario's 2026 budget committed $5.6B for hospital infrastructure and $1.4B for other health infrastructure in 2026-27.4 The project database tracks 258 healthcare projects ($20.5B).1

servicesIndustries.name: Arts, Entertainment & Recreation
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Arts, entertainment, and recreation output was near-flat at -0.1% month-over-month but expanded 2.2% year-over-year in January 2026, with amusement, gambling, and recreation driving growth at +4.6% year-over-year while performing arts, spectator sports, and heritage institutions each contracted 1.1%.1 Information, culture, and recreation combined employment rose 8,800 in the March Labour Force Survey.5 Ontario arts, entertainment, and recreation employed 177,700 in 2024 with moderate to slow growth expected through 2027.3

Vancouver's FIFA 2026 hosting requirements are estimated to necessitate 20,000 incremental hotel rooms for peak demand, mobilizing more than US$1B in hotel-related infrastructure — a requirement that cross-references accommodation (NAICS 72) and construction (NAICS 23) sector activity.4 The Canada Arts Presentation Fund opened applications April 1, and the Toronto Arts Council Strategic Funding deadline passed April 13 with grants up to $30,000 per project.2 The project database tracks 150 tourism and culture projects ($22.3B), of which 94 are under construction and 14 are in proposed status.1

servicesIndustries.name: Accommodation & Food Services
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Accommodation and food services output expanded 0.7% month-over-month and 2.3% year-over-year in January 2026, with a pronounced split between the accommodation and food segments.1 Accommodation services grew 7.7% year-over-year, one of the highest subsector growth rates across all 20 tracked NAICS industries, while food services and drinking places were near-flat at +0.4%.1 The Canada hospitality market was valued at US$21.34B in 2026, with a forecast trajectory to US$27.46B by 2031 at a 5.18% CAGR.2

Employment in the sector declined 10,000 (-0.9%) in the March Labour Force Survey, diverging from the GDP growth trajectory and indicating persistent labour supply constraints.3 The foodservice industry generated a record $120B in sales in 2024, with approximately 1.9 million Canadians employed in hospitality — roughly 9.5% of total employment.2 The sector vacancy rate stood at 3.8% with approximately 18,230 unfilled positions as of 2024.2 Ontario holds 29.75% of the national hospitality market share, while British Columbia is the fastest-growing province at a 5.85% CAGR.2

servicesIndustries.name: Other Services (except Public Administration)
servicesIndustries.analysis:
Other services output grew 0.2% month-over-month and 0.3% year-over-year in January 2026, the smallest absolute movement in the 20-NAICS table.1 Despite the near-flat GDP reading, the sector posted the largest March Labour Force Survey employment gain at +15,000 jobs, indicating demand for repair, personal care, and civic organization services is expanding faster than the output measure captures.2 Repair and maintenance contracted 0.8% year-over-year in GDP terms, personal and laundry services grew 0.4%, and religious, grantmaking, and civic organizations expanded 1.0%.1

High costs for new vehicles continued to drive consumers toward repair and maintenance of existing vehicles, supporting demand in the repair subsector even as its GDP reading lagged.3 Personal care services saw demand support as headline CPI decelerated to 1.8% year-over-year and household disposable income conditions stabilized at the BoC rate of 2.25%.1 British Columbia's 2026 budget expanded the provincial sales tax to professional services, affecting portions of NAICS 81 operating in the province.4 If vehicle cost inflation persists and consumers continue choosing repair over replacement, the repair and maintenance subsector would see sustained demand, potentially narrowing the gap between employment growth and GDP output.3,4

servicesIndustries.analysis:
Public administration output declined 0.1% month-over-month but expanded 0.7% year-over-year in January 2026, with a divergence between the contracting federal subsector and expanding provincial and municipal tiers.1 Federal government public administration contracted 3.2% year-over-year, while provincial and territorial administration grew 2.3% and local, municipal, and regional administration expanded 3.2%.1 The 2026-27 Main Estimates present $502.8B in total budgetary spending ($230.4B voted, $272.4B statutory), with full supply authorization expected in June 2026.2

PM Carney announced a 70% domestic procurement mandate for military spending, specifying Canadian steel, aluminum, and lumber as primary inputs, with a stand-alone defence investment agency expected via spring legislation.3 Defence procurements in the pipeline include submarines on an accelerated timeline, ground-based air defence at CFB Gagetown ($127M infrastructure), Arctic over-the-horizon radar, and early warning surveillance aircraft.4 An audit published April 16 flagged persistent bureaucratic hurdles in military procurement despite the sector evolving rapidly.3 Public Services and Procurement Canada's 2026-27 plan sets $5.93B in total spending with 17,449 FTEs.5 The project database tracks 231 government and defence projects ($165.0B), of which 153 are in proposed status and 40 are under construction.1

industry_executive_summary:
Canada's goods-producing industries recorded a mixed January 2026 GDP print, with mining and oil/gas extraction gaining +1.2% month-over-month and construction rising +1.1%, while manufacturing contracted -1.4% month-over-month and -4.6% year-over-year, the steepest annual decline among goods sectors. Agriculture posted the strongest annual reading across all 20 industries at +5.4% year-over-year, though month-over-month output fell -1.4% amid China's 75.8% duty on Canadian canola seed.

The oil price whipsaw dominated the mining and energy landscape: Brent crude dropped from approximately US$107/bbl to US$90.38/bbl over the two-week window, while WTI collapsed over 34% from its April 2 peak to US$83.85/bbl following the Strait of Hormuz ceasefire. The project database tracks 63 oil and gas projects ($100.2B) and 367 mining projects ($159.5B) with direct commodity price exposure. Construction GDP growth was supported by the $51B Build Communities Strong Fund, launched April 7, with heavy and civil engineering recording +5.8% year-over-year, though housing starts fell 6.0% month-over-month to 235,852 SAAR.

Manufacturing sales rebounded 3.6% to $71.2B in February, led by transportation equipment at +18.8%, while unfilled orders reached a record $117.6B. The restructured U.S. Section 232 tariffs, effective April 6, imposed 50% duties on steel, aluminum, and copper articles. On the services side, the Canadian Sovereign AI Compute Strategy committed up to $700M for compute capacity and $1B for public supercomputing, generating cross-sector demand across NAICS 23 and NAICS 51. Management of companies (NAICS 55) recorded the deepest annual contraction at -21.9% year-over-year, while finance and insurance and information/cultural industries tied for the strongest services reading at +3.2% year-over-year.

commodity_commentary: The two-week commodity tape was dominated by the Strait of Hormuz crisis and its resolution — WTI crude swung from US$80.56 to a peak near US$128/bbl before collapsing to US$83.85 on the April 17 reopening, while Brent followed a parallel path from its 52-week high of US$118.35 down to US$90.38504797. Precious metals advanced on safe-haven flows, with gold reaching US$4,816/oz on April 16 — a new intra-period high — and silver climbing above US$80/oz1819. Base metals tracked China's Q1 GDP beat of 5.0% and March import surge of +27.8%, with copper gaining 3.32% to US$6.07/lb and nickel rising 4.81% month-over-month to US$17,985/tonne495395. Henry Hub natural gas fell to US$2.67/MMBtu, a 17-month low, on elevated storage and mild demand52. Agriculture was mixed: wheat advanced 4.7% on global supply concerns while the Nutrien potash proxy declined 3.56%135. wcs_analysis.narrative: The WCS discount widened to US$16.25/bbl below WTI on April 13, up from US$15.55 on April 11. With the Strait of Hormuz reopening on April 17 sending WTI to US$83.85, the implied WCS level dropped to approximately US$67.60 (US$83.85 minus US$16.25), which if sustained would compress netbacks for heavy crude producers and place additional pressure on the 63 oil and gas projects ($100.2B) tracked in the database.

consumer_pulse:
The Bloomberg-Nanos Consumer Confidence Index declined to 46.93 in the week ended April 3, an 11-month low, down from 47.50 in the prior period.43 The expectations sub-index lost nearly 10 points over four weeks, a deterioration linked to the Iran war entering its sixth week, elevated energy prices from the Strait of Hormuz disruption, and rising inflation concerns.43 Gasoline prices — driven by WTI swinging between $80.56 and $117.63 over the two-week coverage window — were the dominant cost-of-living concern in consumer sentiment tracking.50

Headline CPI at +1.8% year-over-year remains within the Bank of Canada's target band, but component dispersion is wide: food CPI ran at +5.3%, shelter CPI at +1.5%, and energy CPI at -14.2% — a figure that predates the oil price surge and is expected to shift materially in the March CPI release on April 20.145154 Provincial CPI ranges from PE at +7.3% to ON at -1.8%, a 9.1 percentage-point spread.145 Average hourly wages at $37.73 (+4.7% year-over-year) outpaced headline CPI by 2.9 percentage points, though workers aged 15-24 recorded only +1.8% wage growth, trailing inflation in food-heavy consumption baskets.148

Retail sales rose 1.1% to $70.7B in January, with the advance February estimate at +0.9%.143 Housing affordability remained a persistent theme: the MLS HPI fell for a 16th consecutive month, national average home price stood at $673,084 (-0.8% year-over-year), and CREA downgraded its sales forecast citing the oil shock while maintaining a +1.5% annual price gain projection to $688,955.3967 National inventory reached 5 months of supply.67

marketCommentary:
The Strait of Hormuz crisis and ceasefire dominated the two-week period ending April 13, whipsawing commodity prices while equities advanced — WTI crude collapsed 34% from a peak near US$128/bbl (Apr 2) to US$83.85 after the strait reopened Apr 1797, while Brent dropped 9.0% in a single session to US$90.3847. The S&P/TSX Composite rose 1.7% to ~34,052 (+41% Y/Y)46, and the S&P 500 posted a record close at 7,022.9594. The Canadian dollar strengthened 1.5% to 0.7305 CAD/USD44 as the DXY fell toward 98, and the Bank of Canada held at 2.25% for a seventh consecutive meeting61. The project database tracks 7,344 projects valued at $1.37 trillion.

The oil price reversal split the pipeline’s commodity exposure in two directions — 63 oil and gas projects ($100.2B) carry direct WTI exposure, with the WCS differential widening to $16.25/bbl below WTI on Apr 132. On the metals side, gold reached US$4,728/oz (+2.82%)18 and copper climbed to US$6.07/lb (+3.32%)49, referenced by 364 mining projects totalling $159.5B. The 10-year Government of Canada bond yield stood at 3.47%45 with the 2-year at 2.80%42, a 67-basis-point spread, against 211 residential ($44.4B) and 1,671 infrastructure projects ($179.0B) carrying financing cost exposure to rate movements.
